articles.title: South Sudan postpones first-ever national elections until February
articles.text:
South Sudan postpones first-ever national elections until February | Elections News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Young men and boys who fled drought in South Sudan are seen in Torit, the capital of Eastern Equatoria state, South Sudan [File: Juma Peter/AP Photo]
By Al Jazeera Staff and AFP
Published On 14 Nov 202614 Nov 2026
South Sudan has delayed its first-ever presidential and parliamentary elections until February, the latest in a series of delays to the long-sought vote, as ethnic and political tensions deepen.
The country’s election commission announced on Saturday that the polls would be held on February 11 next year, instead of December 22 this year. It did not give any reason for the decision.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 South Sudan’s Kiir dissolves government ahead of first national elections
list 2 of 3 In maps and charts: South Sudan’s 15 years of independence
list 3 of 3 At least 26 killed in clashes along Sudan-South Sudan border regionend of list
The world’s youngest country, which continues to grapple with violence despite a 2018 peace deal that ended five years of civil war, has delayed the vote at least three times since setting 2022 as its election year.
In September, South Sudan’s President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government and appointed a caretaker administration. That step allowed the country to move towards elections without first completing a permanent constitution or census – two processes that were previously tied to the transition.
But analysts and watchdogs warned that move dismantled a key power-sharing arrangement, consolidating power in Kiir’s hands and raising the risk of renewed widespread conflict.
“This amounts to a constitutional coup through legislative reforms,” Yasmin Sooka, chair of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan, said in October.
“Whether elections take place or not, South Sudan will still need an inclusive political settlement, protection for civilians and institutions capable of preventing further violence,” she added.
Kiir’s government forces and followers of detained former Vice President Riek Machar have been involved in escalating, deadly confrontations in recent months.
Advertisement
Other ethnic tensions and cattle-rustling battles have also complicated the picture in one of the world’s poorest countries.
South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011, but Kiir’s and Machar’s forces fought a civil war from 2013 to 2018 that killed at least 400,000 people.
Machar has been under house arrest since last March, accused of crimes against humanity.
Thousands mobilised for registration drive
Under the new election timetable, voter registration is due to begin on Saturday, November 14 and continue until November 28.
A 45-day election campaign period will run from December 27 to February 9, followed by a one-day silence period before the February 11 poll.
Gabriel Bol Deng, chairman of the National Elections Commission, said a total of 3,161 registration centres have been set up across the country, with more than 22,000 staff recruited for the operation.
According to the World Bank, about 90 percent of South Sudan’s 15 million inhabitants have no state-recognised identification, complicating their registration.
Such people, particularly in rural areas, will be identified by community leaders and issued an “identification form” enabling them to vote, Deng said.

articles.title: Nearly $20m found in Hungary’s forests, buildings amid corruption probe
articles.text:
Nearly $20m found in Hungary’s forests, buildings amid corruption probe | Corruption News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar, shown in Brussels on May 29, 2026, has launched investigations into corruption under his predecessor, Viktor Orban [File: Virginia Mayo/AP]
By Al Jazeera Staff, AP and Reuters
Published On 14 Nov 202614 Nov 2026
Hungarian investigators have found $19.5m in hidden cash, including bundles dug out in forests, during a corruption probe involving a former minister under ex-Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, a new agency set up to investigate suspected misuse of public money, said in a statement late on Friday that searches took place on November 12 and 13 in Budapest and three other parts of Hungary.
Recommended Stories list of 2 items
list 1 of 2 Moscow announces sudden death of Russia’s envoy to US
list 2 of 2 Regional security dominates European talks in Dublin amid hybrid attacksend of list
Its investigators found Hungarian forints, euros and US dollars in farm buildings, warehouses, a home and “a high-value safe in a secluded location”, as well as beneath the ground in forests. The agency released footage showing officers digging outdoors after dark and examining piles of cash, which was later deposited with the state treasury.
Finance Minister Andras Karman said on Facebook on Friday that 12 treasury employees spent eight hours counting it.
The discovery comes amid an investigation into Miklos Sesztak, Hungary’s development minister from 2014 to 2018, who is suspected of receiving more than $37.2m in bribes and kickbacks tied to overpriced secondhand bus purchases by a state transport company and government construction projects.
He was detained in September and denies wrongdoing.
Prime Minister Peter Magyar, whose centre-right, pro-European Tisza party ended Orban’s 16 years in power in April, said on Facebook on Friday that the recovery signalled the end of what he called the “Fidesz-KDNP mafia”.
Fidesz is Orban’s right-wing party, while KDNP, the Christian Democratic People’s Party, was its smaller governing ally.
Advertisement
Orban has previously accused the new government of using the investigations to force him out of politics.
Other former ministers have been arrested in separate cases, as has Gyorgy Matolcsy, the former governor of Hungary’s central bank, which sets monetary policy.
His case concerns alleged misuse of public assets held by a central bank foundation. Matolcsy has denied wrongdoing.
A survey published this week by Hungarian news website HVG by pollster Median suggested that 70 percent of respondents considered investigating suspected corruption under Orban and holding those responsible accountable very important.

articles.title: UN says 25 seafarers killed in, around Hormuz since US-Israel war on Iran
articles.text:
UN says 25 seafarers killed in, around Hormuz since US-Israel war on Iran | US-Israel war on Iran News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on November 9 [Reuters]
By Al Jazeera Staff
Published On 14 Nov 202614 Nov 2026
At least 25 seafarers have been killed in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the US-Israeli war on Iran broke out in February, according to the United Nations.
Khaled Khiari, assistant secretary-general for the Middle East, Asia and the Pacific, gave the figures, which cover the period up to November 11, during a UN Security Council briefing on Friday.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Why is Trump saying ‘no deal necessary’ with Iran as he sidelines JD Vance?
list 2 of 3 Iran threatens unlimited response over Strait of Hormuz after US attack
list 3 of 3 The Gulf must build security that can outlast this warend of list
“This situation cannot be allowed to become the new normal,” said Khiari, urging the “full restoration of maritime navigation in the region”.
He pointed out that security incidents in and around Hormuz have been rising, with October recording the highest tally since the start of the conflict.
The UN’s International Maritime Organization (IMO) tracked 136 security incidents involving vessels in Hormuz and the wider Middle East between March 1 and November 11. It said 35 of those incidents came in October and 10 in November.
“Every day brings new reports of maritime incidents,” said Khiari. “These incidents are unacceptable,” he added. “Civilian vessels and commercial shipping must not become targets.”
His remarks come as Iranian authorities on Saturday reported that three oil tankers had hit mines while travelling through “unauthorised” or “restricted” areas of Hormuz, catching fire.
Tehran has warned vessels that they must receive Iranian approval to cross the waterway during the conflict, and has repeatedly attacked ships accused of violating its protocol.
“Any offending tanker that travels in the restricted area east of the Strait of Hormuz will be set on fire by hitting naval mines,” Iran’s navy warned in a statement carried by the country’s IRIB broadcaster.
Iranian officials have insisted the strait will not be open until the US meets its demands, which include an end to the US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, the lifting of economic sanctions, the release of Iranian frozen funds, ending fighting on all fronts, and an explicit announcement of an end to the war.
Advertisement
The US military claims it has cleared the strait’s main routes of mines and that the waterway is open for commercial shipping.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is approximately 65 percent below pre-war levels, according to the latest report from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
Khiari, in his remarks to the UN Security Council, said “the present maritime arrangements in the Middle East remain costly, unpredictable, and unsafe”.
“Disruptions to maritime navigation continue to have significant global economic consequences, driving up energy, transport and insurance costs, fuelling inflation and threatening food security amid severely constrained fertiliser shipments.”

articles.title: US air travel in chaos after rare nationwide ground stop halts flights
articles.text:
US air travel thrown into chaos after nationwide ground stop halts flights | Aviation News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Travelers wait at a United airlines terminal as flights are delayed at Los Angeles international airport on November 13, 2026 [Ethan Swope/AP Photo]
By Al Jazeera Staff and The Associated Press
Published On 14 Nov 202614 Nov 2026
More than 1.5 million air passengers have faced travel disruption after the United States halted departing flights nationwide for more than four hours, with airlines warning they would take days to recover.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted the ground stop at 8:15pm Eastern time on Friday (01:15 GMT on Saturday), after a telecommunications outage affected the country’s 22 regional air traffic control centres. FlightRadar24 counted more than 4,700 cancellations and 10,000 delays on Friday, with 700 flights already cancelled for Saturday.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Microsoft hit by global outages: What happened and why?
list 2 of 3 FAA ground stop lifted: Why were US flights grounded, and what’s next?
list 3 of 3 US agencies unite to combat rogue drone threats nationwideend of list
At Los Angeles airport, passenger Nicholas Erdodi, who had travelled from New Zealand to attend a conference in Chicago, told Al Jazeera he had spent six hours at the airport after being forced off his plane.
“The challenge is you cannot ask anyone here what to do,” he said. “The lack of information is what bothers me.” He had been rebooked, but was unsure whether his next flight would go.
Others affected included sport teams in the NBA, NHL and college football.
Todd Curtis, an aviation safety expert and chief executive of AirSafe.com, told Al Jazeera that the failures appeared to be concentrated in the country’s air route traffic control centres.
“There are 21 across the United States, one in Alaska and the other 20 in the lower 48,” he said.
“These are the folks who handle the aircraft that are transiting from one part of the country to the other, and they rely on multiple handoffs between controllers.”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, centre left, and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, centre right, speak during a news conference in the James Brady Briefing Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on November 13, 2026 [Alex Brandon/AP]
US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said it would “take us some time” to restore capacity and that “we’re going to have some makeup to do.”
Advertisement
He acknowledged that tens of thousands of travellers had been stranded, saying he expected operations to be back to normal for the Thanksgiving rush, which begins in less than two weeks.
Cirium, an aviation analytics firm, said about 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to depart US airports after 4pm Eastern time (21:00 GMT), and that at least 827 flights had been diverted by 7:05pm on Friday (00:05 am on Saturday).
Sports weekend in chaos
The Associated Press news agency reported that the shutdown left NBA, NHL and college teams stranded, with NFL teams wondering whether they could travel in time for their games.
The Nets were among five NBA teams scheduled to fly on Friday for Saturday games. There are 14 NHL games set to play Saturday.
The San Jose Sharks were left waiting to fly to Utah, while the Florida Panthers reached St Louis before the stoppage. The Texas Longhorns had boarded their plane before it was grounded. “We are grounded and waiting to see when we can leave,” a team spokesman said.
If they have to take a bus to Baton Rouge, the trip for Saturday’s 6:30pm kickoff would take about seven hours.
Planes are parked at Harry Reid international airport in Las Vegas during a nationwide ground stop on November 13, 2026 [John Locher/AP]
Airlines and airports
Delta Air Lines said it was “safely resuming operations”, offering flexible rebooking, and warned that repositioning aircraft and crews would take time.
United Airlines said it was resuming a number of Friday night flights.
JetBlue plans to resume on Saturday morning.
Air Canada said operations would return gradually, with disruption likely on Saturday, and Aeromexico was working to resume operations.
In Mexico City, the Benito Juarez international airport said about 70 flights scheduled for Friday could be affected.
In Canada, Toronto Pearson said flights that did not need to cross US airspace were operating as normal and that it had increased staffing to support affected passengers.
Advertisement

articles.title: Philippine court orders arrest of jailed, US-wanted celebrity preacher
articles.text:
Philippine court orders arrest of jailed, US-wanted celebrity preacher | Religion News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Religious leader Apollo Quiboloy, who is wanted by the US FBI for child trafficking and other crimes, attends the oathtaking of Sara Duterte as the next vice president on June 19, 2022 in Davao, the Philippines [Ezra Acayan/Getty Images]
By Al Jazeera Staff and AFP
Published On 14 Nov 202614 Nov 2026
A Philippine court has ordered the arrest of jailed celebrity preacher Apollo Quiboloy, who is wanted in the US on child sex trafficking charges, in a step towards his possible extradition, according to the country’s Justice Department.
The department’s spokesman Polo Martinez told the AFP news agency on Saturday that the Makati Regional Trial Court issued the warrant of arrest and a hold-departure on Thursday after finding probable cause that he committed the offences charged.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 War, tariffs and China: What the US midterms mean for the Asia-Pacific
list 2 of 3 Which countries and industries emit the most greenhouse gases?
list 3 of 3 Microsoft hit by global outages: What happened and why?end of list
The Philippine government filed its petition with a lower court on Monday, three months after Washington formally requested his extradition in August. Under Philippine law, the court must now hold hearings before deciding whether or not to hand him over.
The court issued the same orders against two co-accused, Teresita Dandan and Helen Panilag, both officers of Quiboloy’s Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) sect. The two women are still at large, according to local media reports.
Palace Press Officer Claire Castro, speaking on behalf of the Office of the President, denied that the warrant was timed to coincide with US President Donald Trump’s visit to Manila on November 17 for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.
“No, it was probably just a coincidence,” she said, according to the Philippines News Agency.
Quiboloy, who calls himself the “appointed son of God”, is being held without bail while on trial for human trafficking in Pasig, which carries life in prison if convicted, AFP reported.
He also faces a child abuse trial in Quezon City, according to local media. He has denied the allegations and pleaded not guilty to the Philippine charges.
Advertisement
US charges
A US grand jury indicted Quiboloy in 2021 for conspiracy to engage in sex trafficking by force, fraud and coercion, sex trafficking of children and bulk cash smuggling, AFP reported.
The FBI identified Dandan as the “international administrator” of a fake charity operation, and Panilag as a former top church administrator in the US, according to local media reports.
Police said after his 2024 arrest that alleged victims were told they were having sex with the “spirit of God” and were threatened that “angels of death” would hunt them down if they told anyone, AFP reported.
The church said at the time that members had “freedom of choice”.
Quiboloy’s sect claims to have millions of followers and owns a television network.
He is a close ally of former President Rodrigo Duterte. He ran for Senate last year from prison and received 5.6 million votes, but lost, AFP reported.

articles.title: FAA ground stop lifted: Why were US flights grounded, and what’s next?
articles.text:
FAA ground stop lifted: Why were US flights grounded, and what’s next? | Aviation News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
FAA grounds all fights across the US over ‘telecommunication outage’
By Elizabeth Melimopoulos
Published On 14 Nov 202614 Nov 2026|
Updated: 5 hours agoUpdated: 5 hours ago
The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has lifted a nationwide ground stop imposed on Friday that halted departing flights, an order it issued citing “extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety”.
The halt, which grounded thousands of flights across the country, was lifted on Friday evening after five hours, making it the longest ground stop in 25 years.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 US flights resume after FAA lifts hours-long nationwide ground stop
list 2 of 3 FAA grounds all fights across the US over ‘telecommunication outage’
list 3 of 3 Former FAA official says ‘nobody really knows what is going on’end of list
It was also the second nationwide ground stop of all departures since the September 11, 2001, attacks.
“Everybody’s safe,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, adding that this was not “another 9/11” and that there were no suspected cyberattacks.
Here is what we know:
What happened?
The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop at 3:54pm Eastern Time (20:54 GMT) on Friday due to a telecommunications outage affecting air route traffic control centres, which handle flights travelling across the country.
The FAA confirmed that the nationwide ground stop had been lifted.
US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said airspace reopened at 8:15pm ET (01:15 GMT on Saturday), after more than four hours of disruption.
“We’ve opened up the airspace,” Duffy said, warning that flights would not resume immediately.
“It’s going to be slow,” he added, urging passengers to check with their airlines.
Duffy said flights would resume depending on the availability of pilots and flight attendants, with authorities trying to get as many flights moving as possible on Friday night.
Aviation analytics firm Cirium said that after 4pm ET (21:00 GMT) on Friday, about 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers were still scheduled to depart from US airports.
Advertisement
By 7:05pm ET (00:05 GMT on Saturday), at least 827 flights had been diverted, according to Cirium. Of those, 670 returned to their departure airports, while 157 were diverted elsewhere.
Aircraft already in the air were allowed to continue to their destinations and land during the ground stop.
During the ground stop, international flights were handled on a case-by-case basis, with some allowed to depart despite the restrictions.
How many flights were affected?
More than 4,700 flights were cancelled and 10,000 delayed on Friday, while another 700 had already been cancelled for Saturday, according to FlightRadar24.
Aviation analysts said it could take days for airlines to restore their schedules.
Reporting from Los Angeles international airport, Al Jazeera’s John Hendren spoke to passenger Nicholas Erdodi, who travelled from New Zealand and was trying to reach Chicago for a conference.
Erdodi said he had been travelling for 16 to 18 hours before spending another six hours at the airport, where passengers had been forced to leave their plane.
“The challenge is you cannot ask anyone here what to do,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Lack of information is what bothers me, I mean, and not to mention find the hotel for the night, not to mention all the cost.”
Erdodi said he had been rebooked but remained uncertain whether his next flight would depart.
“I work in tech, I understand what could be going on, but someone needs to tell us,” he said.
“It doesn’t matter if someone tells us that we don’t know what’s happening, but please just let us know what’s going on,” he added.
What does a nationwide ground stop mean?
A nationwide ground stop temporarily requires departing aircraft to remain on the ground until cleared to take off.
Flights in the air are generally allowed to continue to their destination, but new departures are on strict orders to stay grounded.
The measure is intended to stop any further aircraft from entering the airspace as the authorities deal with the safety issues.
What caused the FAA nationwide ground stop?
The FAA said the ground stop was caused by a telecommunications outage affecting air traffic control systems.
Duffy said the outage was caused by switches and routers that became overloaded with data and went down, adding that the incident did not involve a total loss of communications or radar capabilities.
Tony Stanton, a former senior executive with Australia’s Civil Aviation Safety Authority, told Al Jazeera that a US government report published in September warned about problems with the aviation infrastructure before these latest disruptions.
Advertisement
The report, from the Government Accountability Office (GAO), highlighted ageing copper cables dating back to the 1960s and warned that delays in modernising the system could lead to further disruptions.
It also noted that while the FAA was trying to implement changes, officials were prioritising speeding up the process and failing to properly schedule changes, meaning switches were often happening at the same time and overwhelming the system.
On Friday, officials admitted that new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated parts of it and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps.
Where was most impacted?
Todd Curtis, an aviation safety expert and chief executive of AirSafe.com, told Al Jazeera that the failures appeared to be concentrated in the country’s air route traffic control centres.
“There are 21 across the United States, one in Alaska and the other 20 in the lower 48,” he said.
“These are the folks who handle the aircraft that are transiting from one part of the country to the other, and they rely on multiple handoffs between controllers.”

articles.title: Trump, Xi and Putin to hold first three-way summit in China
articles.text:
Trump, Xi and Putin to hold first three-way summit in China | Nuclear Weapons News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
From left: US President Donald Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's President Vladimir Putin [File: AP Photo]
By Al Jazeera Staff, AP and Reuters
Published On 14 Nov 202614 Nov 2026
Leaders of the United States, China and Russia are set to hold an unprecedented three-way meeting next week, the White House has said.
US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China’s tech hub, the White House assistant press secretary confirmed in an announcement.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 The real winner in Poland’s constitutional battle is Putin
list 2 of 3 EU agrees on five countries to represent Europe in Ukraine peace talks
list 3 of 3 Afghanistan’s new road to China ends at a closed borderend of list
The talks will be held nine months after the last nuclear arms treaty between Washington and Moscow expired, leaving the world’s two countries with the largest atomic arsenals without caps for the first time in more than 50 years.
What’s on the agenda?
Trump has said the meeting is a chance for all three countries to reach a deal on nuclear stockpiles.
The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) lapsed in February. Trump then rejected Russia’s proposal to extend it for another year and demanded a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes China.
Expectations are low. “We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior Trump administration official told the Reuters news agency, describing the meeting as the start of a conversation.
Russia holds the most nuclear warheads, followed by the US, then China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
Trump plans on discussing the Iran war with Xi and Putin, but will steer away from discussing Russia’s war in Ukraine, according to a senior US official who briefed reporters on condition of anonymity.
Advertisement
Elon Musk will also travel with Trump to China but will not attend the meeting, the official added. Trump is also not expected to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during the Asia trip.
Yalta Conference comparisons
The planned summit has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the US, Britain and the Soviet Union shaped the post-war order.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, however, dismissed the parallel, saying any agreements reached in Shenzhen cannot be imposed on others, but he still called the meeting “extremely significant”.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has voiced concern that the meeting could become a platform to discuss a Ukraine deal behind Kyiv’s back.
Trump has pursued closer ties with both leaders despite a short-lived trade war with China last year and Russia’s continuing war in Ukraine, where Washington is seeking to mediate a solution.
Advertisement
